pedagogy.summary: Children learn to recognise and DRAW shapes that satisfy a specified attribute (e.g. exactly five sides, a given number of angles) and to identify triangles, quadrilaterals, pentagons and hexagons within a mixed set. The procedural work is building or selecting to a property — a pentagon is any closed figure with five straight sides — rather than reproducing a memorised prototype. The central obstacle is the prototype effect: children draw and accept only the regular, symmetrical, 'textbook' version and miss irregular or rotated members of the class. Best taught by generating many varied and irregular examples, defining each class by its attribute, and hunting for ALL members (including non-prototypical ones) in mixed sets.
bestPractices: Define each shape class by its attribute (a hexagon is ANY closed shape with 6 straight sides / 6 vertices) and check drawn shapes against it.
Demand and celebrate IRREGULAR and rotated examples — 'draw a different pentagon that doesn't look like that one' — to break the single-prototype image.
Give mixed 'find them all' sets that include irregular, tilted and near-miss shapes so identifying a class means applying the attribute, not matching a picture.
Model counting and marking each side/vertex once when drawing or checking, so the side-count is accurate.
Use dotted paper, geoboards or a peg grid to support accurate drawing of straight-sided closed figures.
keyRepresentations: Geoboard / pegboard and dotted paper for constructing polygons to a target side-count
Mixed shape sets containing regular, irregular, tilted and near-miss examples plus non-examples
Side/vertex tally marks made while counting
Side-by-side regular vs irregular pentagon/hexagon to show both satisfy the attribute
commonMisconceptions: Draws or accepts only the prototypical regular, symmetrical, horizontal-base example and misses irregular or rotated members of a class.
Miscounts sides or vertices when drawing or identifying (draws six sides when asked for five; loses track counting an irregular shape).
Draws a non-closed figure or one with curved sides, not attending to 'closed' and 'straight-sided'.
Judges class membership by the name/look ('that's not a quadrilateral, it's a diamond') rather than by counting the sides.

learn.summary: Children learn to draw and identify polygons by their defining attribute — a pentagon is ANY closed figure with five straight sides whose sides do not cross each other, not one memorised 'textbook' shape. The core obstacle is the prototype effect: learners draw and accept only the regular, symmetrical, horizontal-base version and miss irregular, tilted or rotated members of a class. Guidance centres on generating many varied and irregular examples, defining each class by its attribute (side/vertex count, closed, straight-sided, sides not crossing), and hunting for ALL members in mixed sets that include non-prototypical and near-miss shapes. Accurate side/vertex counting is scaffolded by marking each once.

activities.title: Build a polygon to a target side-count
feedback: If the shape has the wrong number of sides, recount together, marking each side exactly once from a clear start point; dotted paper or pegs keep sides straight.
If only a regular/symmetrical version is produced, prompt: 'Make one that is squished, tilted, or spiky but still has five straight sides' and affirm that it counts just as much.
If the figure has a gap or a curved/bulging edge, check it against the attributes aloud: is it closed? is every side straight?
Celebrate an irregular valid solution explicitly so the learner sees it is as correct as the neat one.
activities.rationale: Constructing to an attribute is an active production task that confronts the prototype effect directly; demanding varied and irregular examples is intended to break the single-image definition. Counting sides, checking closure (whether by the learner, an adult, or an optional live side-counter) and visibly accepting ANY valid (including irregular) shape are intended to make the defining attribute the thing being rewarded.
sourceClaims: A polygon is a 2-D shape made of three or more straight sides that meet at vertices; children are taught to identify and sort polygons by number of sides/vertices, using varied examples (all sides/vertices the same, some the same, all different). A common misconception is inaccurate counting of sides/vertices from losing track of the start point; remedy is to mark each side/vertex once as it is counted.

The instructional goal is to analyse shapes by defining properties (e.g. a triangle has three straight sides and is closed), invariant to size, orientation and colour, rather than by holistic appearance.
learnerActions: Given an instruction such as 'build a shape with exactly five straight sides', construct the figure on dotted paper, a geoboard, or a peg/rubber-band grid.
Count and mark each side (and vertex) once as it is drawn, so the total is checked rather than guessed.
Ensure the figure CLOSES and that every side is straight before declaring it finished.
When one valid shape is made, draw 'a different pentagon that does NOT look like the first one' — a long, spiky, or irregular one.
Compare a regular and an irregular example of the same class side by side and state why both satisfy the attribute.
activities.intendedInsight: A polygon class is defined by its attribute (number of straight sides meeting at vertices, closed figure with sides that do not cross), invariant to size, orientation and regularity — not by matching a single remembered prototype.

activities.title: Find them all in a mixed set
feedback: If an irregular or tilted member is skipped, draw attention to it and recount its sides together; attending to the awkward four-sided shape is intended to loosen the prototype grip as the learner sees the squished one also counts.
If a shape is included or excluded by its name/look alone (e.g. 'that's a diamond, not a quadrilateral'), redirect to counting the four straight sides.
If counting on an irregular shape loses track, model starting at one vertex and marking each side once around the figure.
activities.rationale: A 'find them all' set that deliberately contains non-prototypical and near-miss shapes is designed to require attribute-based classification and to surface the prototype misconception; it is hard to fake because the regular example alone is insufficient to complete the task.
sourceClaims: Young children over-rely on a prototypical exemplar: 93-96% identify a prototypical (equilateral, horizontal-base) triangle but far fewer accept atypical types (only ~30.5% identified all three of scalene/right/isosceles) or rotated versions; a non-formal attribute matching the prototype (e.g. horizontal base) is treated as defining ('imposed attribute'). Remedy: typical + atypical examples and non-examples.

The instructional goal is to analyse shapes by defining properties (e.g. a triangle has three straight sides and is closed), invariant to size, orientation and colour, rather than by holistic appearance.
learnerActions: From a mixed set that includes regular, irregular, tilted, rotated and near-miss shapes plus non-examples, mark EVERY member of a named class (e.g. 'circle all the quadrilaterals').
For each shape marked or skipped, justify by counting sides/vertices and checking closed + straight-sided, not by its name or look.
Deliberately inspect the awkward shapes — a long thin tilted four-sided shape, a dented pentagon — and decide membership by the attribute.
Explain why a square is a quadrilateral, and why a 'diamond' is also a quadrilateral regardless of its orientation.
activities.intendedInsight: Identifying a class means applying its attribute to every candidate, including irregular and rotated ones, rather than recognising a familiar picture.

activities.title: Name, draw and justify by attribute
feedback: If the count is wrong, recount marking each side/vertex once; dotted paper keeps the sides straight.
If both drawings look the same, ask for a genuinely different-looking version with the same number of sides.
Accept and praise any closed, straight-sided figure with the correct count regardless of regularity.
activities.rationale: Requiring a spoken/written justification by attribute, plus a deliberately varied second example, checks that the class is defined by count rather than appearance.
sourceClaims: The instructional goal is to analyse shapes by defining properties (e.g. a triangle has three straight sides and is closed), invariant to size, orientation and colour, rather than by holistic appearance.

A polygon is a 2-D shape made of three or more straight sides that meet at vertices; children are taught to identify and sort polygons by number of sides/vertices, using varied examples (all sides/vertices the same, some the same, all different). A common misconception is inaccurate counting of sides/vertices from losing track of the start point; remedy is to mark each side/vertex once as it is counted.
learnerActions: Draw a named polygon (e.g. a hexagon) and explain how you know it is one by counting its six straight sides and six vertices/angles.
Produce a second example of the same name that looks clearly different from the first.
State the defining attributes in your own words ('a hexagon is any closed shape with six straight sides that do not cross each other').
activities.intendedInsight: Justifying class membership by the attribute count — and producing a non-prototypical second example — demonstrates the definition is understood, not just a remembered shape.

constraints: Tasks must require active drawing/construction and selection, not tap-to-reveal recognition: a static labelled picture can show examples but does not itself let the learner build or choose, and active production and selection are where the prototype misconception can surface.
Mixed 'find them all' sets must include irregular, tilted, rotated and near-miss shapes plus non-examples; a set of only regular shapes cannot discriminate attribute-use from picture-matching.

Any 'draw a pentagon' response format should be paired with a side-count check (counting/marking by the learner or an adult), since free drawing alone does not reliably verify the exact number of straight sides.

A fixed single-answer format under-rewards the many-different-valid-answers goal; whatever format is used, multiple distinct correct shapes (including irregular ones) must be treated as equally valid.

A live side-counter, closure check, and visible acceptance of any valid shape (e.g. a highlight on a correct irregular pentagon, a pulse on a missed tilted quadrilateral) are helpful ways to make the mechanism concrete, but are optional illustrations, not required technology.

The topic is primarily 2-D polygon drawing and identification; the single 'cubes' reference does not require a 3-D spatial environment. If cube identification is added, ask about the mathematical solid REPRESENTED on a thin card (which itself has slight thickness and can be held), not whether the physical card can be picked up.
Scaffolds (dotted paper, geoboards, peg grids) support accurate straight sides and counting but should not become the only medium; plain drawing and physical shape sorting are also valid.

probeDeeper: You drew this five-sided shape. Count the sides with me — is it exactly five?
Is THIS a quadrilateral? [show a long, thin, tilted, irregular four-sided shape] How do you know?
Could you draw a completely different pentagon — one that doesn't look like the first?
Is a square a quadrilateral? Why?
assess.correctAnswer: (1) Draws any closed figure with exactly five straight sides — need not be a regular pentagon. (2) Circles every four-sided shape, including irregular and rotated ones, and no others. (3) Draws a six-sided closed figure and justifies by counting six sides (and six vertices/angles). The attribute is satisfied by the count, not by matching a prototype.

errorPatterns.pattern: Draws or accepts only the prototype — a regular, symmetrical, horizontal-base example — and misses irregular or rotated members of the class.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Define the class by its attribute (a quadrilateral is ANY closed shape with four straight sides), then present many varied and irregular examples with non-examples to sort, and ask for a 'different one that doesn't look like that'.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: In the quadrilateral hunt, skips irregular or tilted four-sided shapes; when asked to draw, produces only the textbook-regular version.

errorPatterns.pattern: Miscounts sides or vertices when drawing or identifying — draws six sides when asked for five, or loses track counting an irregular shape.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold: model numbering/marking each side as it is drawn or counted so each is counted exactly once; use dotted paper for accurate straight sides.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The drawn shape has the wrong number of sides; a recount gives a different total.

errorPatterns.pattern: Draws a non-closed figure or one with curved sides, not attending to 'closed' and 'straight-sided'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: State and check the defining attributes — closed, straight sides — against each drawn shape, using the 'is it / is it not a polygon' test.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The drawn polygon has a gap or a bulging/curved side.

responseLevels.gap: Draws or selects only the prototypical regular example, draws the wrong number of sides, or draws non-closed/curved figures — attends to the picture, not the attribute.
responseLevels.full: Draws any closed figure with the exact specified number of straight sides in varied/irregular forms, identifies ALL members of a class including irregular and rotated ones while excluding non-members, and justifies by the defining attribute (SOLO relational, with transfer).
responseLevels.partial: Draws a correct example and identifies prototypical members, but misses irregular or rotated instances (circles the square but not an irregular quadrilateral) or occasionally miscounts sides (SOLO multistructural).

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Set three short tasks and watch how the child works: (1) 'Draw me a shape with exactly five straight sides.' (2) Hand them a mixed set of shapes (including irregular and tilted ones): 'Circle all the quadrilaterals.' (3) 'Draw a hexagon, and show me how you know it is a hexagon.'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching the child draw and select reveals whether they build to the specified attribute or reach for a memorised prototype. The quadrilateral hunt deliberately includes irregular and tilted four-sided shapes: a child who circles only the square/rectangle is matching a picture, while one who circles the awkward ones is applying 'four straight sides'. This is hard to fake because the mixed set contains non-prototypical members.
